summary.text: A quasar is an extremely luminous active galactic nucleus, and it is sometimes called a quasi-stellar object.
Its energy comes from gas falling toward a supermassive black hole, which heats up and releases electromagnetic radiation.
The most powerful quasars shine thousands of times brighter than a galaxy like the Milky Way.

facts.label: Identified so far
facts.value: About a million with reliable spectroscopic redshifts

items.prompt: How does the light output of the most powerful quasars compare with a galaxy like our own?

options.label: About the same
Roughly ten times greater
Thousands of times greater
Millions of times greater

items.explain: The most powerful quasars have luminosities thousands of times greater than a galaxy such as the Milky Way.

items.prompt: Records of 3C 273 showed its brightness varied over about a year. What did that tell astronomers?

options.label: A large share of its light came from a region under a light-year across
Most of its light came from a region far bigger than a galaxy
It was a nearby star flickering
It was shrinking quickly

items.explain: Yearly variability implied that a substantial fraction of the light came from a region less than 1 light-year in size.

items.prompt: The spectrum of 3C 273 turned out to be ordinary hydrogen light shifted toward red. If that shift is due to distance, what does it say about the object?

options.label: It is a dim star close to us
It is an ordinary galaxy a bit nearer
It is a star racing through our galaxy
It is far brighter than any galaxy but much smaller

items.explain: If the redshift was cosmological, the distance implied that 3C 273 was far more luminous than any galaxy but much more compact.

items.prompt: A telescope image shows a quasar. Where would you expect to find it?

options.label: Drifting alone in the space between galaxies
At a galaxy's center, perhaps a merging one
Hidden inside one single ordinary star
Along the very edge of a spiral arm

items.explain: Hubble images show quasars occur in the centers of galaxies, and some host galaxies are interacting or merging.

items.prompt: Surveys of quasars at many distances show how common they were over cosmic history. What do they reveal?

options.label: They are more common now than before
They have appeared at a steady rate always
They only appear in very young galaxies
They were more common in the distant past than they are now

items.explain: Discovery surveys show quasar activity was more common in the distant past.

items.prompt: What is the energy source behind a quasar's glare?

options.label: Gas falling toward a black hole heats up and releases radiation
A huge crowd of young stars burning together
Matter turning into light inside a giant star
A galaxy collision that pushes gas outward

items.explain: Gas in the disc falling towards the supermassive black hole heats up and releases energy as electromagnetic radiation.
